title: Partial GPU fabric failure - fallback checklist (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic checklist for on-call and SREs to handle partial GPU fabric failures (PCIe errors, NVLink flaps, fabric isolated to subset of hosts) where a subset of GPUs or PCIe paths in a rack/node are unreliable but nodes are still reachable. Focus is: fast mitigation, preserve customer workloads, avoid aggressive mass-evacuations, and buy time for controlled replacements/backfill.

Scope and assumptions:
- Targets incidents where "partial fabric" means: repeated ECC/PCIe errors, NVLink peer loss, or device errors that are intermittent or affect only some GPUs on a host, not entire pod/node (not complete host kernel panic).
- We assume Kubernetes with device-plugin (mig/annotated GPUs), node exporter/metrics and Prometheus alerting, and an SRE on-call with access to infra slack (#infra-ops) and runbook.
- For full node kernel panic or hardware offline, follow standard node-failover runbook instead.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm alert context
   - Pull alert: f_gpubus_error, gpu_ecc_rate, nvlink_peer_loss, kubelet_device_plugin_crash
   - Check scope: how many pods, nodes, AZs affected? Use Prometheus/Graphana + `kubectl get pods -A -o wide` filtered to GPU nodes.
2) Isolate severity
   - If >30% of cluster GPU capacity in a region is impacted, escalate to PagerDuty SEV-1 and notify #infra-ops immediately.
   - If single node or single rack (<= 3 nodes) and errors intermittent, treat as SEV-2.
3) Collect forensic artifacts (do these before any disruptive action)
   - `dmesg | tail -n 200` on affected node(s)
   - `journalctl -u nvidia-persistenced -u kubelet -n 500`
   - `kubectl describe pod <gpu-pod>` for failing pods
   - Snapshot of device state: `nvidia-smi -q -d PIDS,ERROR` and `nvidia-smi topo -m`
   - Save to incident ticket and upload to linked artifacts.

Safety and decision rules:
- Avoid immediate cluster-wide eviction. Target affected GPUs/nodes first.
- Prefer soft mitigation (taint/eject GPUs from scheduling) over immediate node cordon/drain unless I/O or kernel instability present.
- If pod GPU allocation cannot be remapped safely (e.g., using MIG), prepare controlled drain with graceful eviction and fallback routing to Dedicated capacity or lower-tier model variants.

Step-by-step fallback checklist (ordered):
A) Soft-disable GPUs on host (non-disruptive if possible)
   - If device-plugin supports per-GPU marking, mark the problematic GPU(s) "unschedulable" with device-plugin annotation (example for nvidia-device-plugin: annotate node with `nvidia.com/gpu: 0` override).
   - If not supported, apply a node-level taint that prevents new GPU scheduling while keeping existing pods running: `kubectl taint nodes <node> gpu-fabric-issue=true:NoSchedule`
   - Notify downstream teams: add short note to incident thread with expected impact.
B) Redirect traffic and avoid cascading failures
   - If a model route depends on these nodes, push policy change: reduce concurrency per-request, enable cached responses for bursty workloads, or route to canary pool (use service/router config).
   - For hosted API customers impacted, if rate-limiting can reduce load to healthy nodes, do so.
C) Eviction plan for pods actively suffering
   - If pods are failing or exhibiting memory corruption, do a targeted eviction per pod: `kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=60` then observe restart and scheduling decisions.
   - If pods are stateful or long-running (e.g., inference servers with large warmup), coordinate with application owner and prefer node drain with `--ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force` only when necessary.
D) Controlled node drain for seriously unstable hosts
   - Cordon node: `kubectl cordon <node>`
   - Drain with graceful windows: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m`
   - Monitor re-scheduling: ensure scheduler routes pods to compatible nodes (check GPU capability/mig profile).
E) Immediate capacity backfill (if drained nodes reduce capacity below SLO)
   - Trigger hot-pool autoscaler (internal tool): `infra scale add --pool=hot-gpu --count=2 --reason="fabric-backfill"`
   - Fallback: move lower-precision quantized model versions to healthy nodes to increase throughput/unit. Communicate with product on risk/perf tradeoff.
F) Kernel/firmware toggles and device resets (non-destructive steps)
   - Soft reset GPU with nvidia-smi if driver indicates recoverable error: `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i <gpu-id>` (only if supported and after checkpointing pod state).
   - Avoid powering down racks remotely unless coordinated with on-site ops.
G) Hardware replacement workflow (when replacement required)
   - Open hardware ticket with partner/vendor with diagnostic logs attached. Use internal HW-TICKET-<id> for tracking.
   - Schedule maintenance window if node removal will impact capacity >10%.
H) Post-incident state and rollback
   - After repair, uncordon node: `kubectl uncordon <node>` and remove taints/annotations.
   - Run smoke tests: small injection workloads, latency/throughput baseline checks, metric sanity (GPU error counters stay at 0 for 30 minutes).

Runbook commands (common snippets)
- list gpu nodes and errors: `for n in $(kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu -o name); do echo $n; ssh $n \"nvidia-smi -q | egrep -i 'ecc|error|pci' -A3\"; done`
- soft-disable scheduling via annotation (example): `kubectl annotate node <node> gpu.redwood/status=partial-fabric-1 --overwrite`
- quick drain with skip: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=90 --timeout=8m`

Notifications and stakeholders:
- Slack channels: #infra-ops (primary), #sre-incident (post), #hosting-ops (if hosted api customers impacted).
- Email or PagerDuty escalation for SEV-1 to: infra-lead, product-ops, customer-success (if SLOs breached).
- Add incident to the board: attach to Linear ticket RED-2147 and tag on-call and owners.

Observability checks to run continuously during incident:
- GPU counters: ECC corrected/uncorrected, PCIe error counts, NVLink peer loss events in Prometheus dashboards.
- Pod-level failures: OOMs, container restarts, readiness probe failures.
- Scheduler events: pending pods due to insufficient GPU resources.
- Customer-facing SLOs: 95p latency and error-rate monitors.

Post-incident follow-up (owner responsibilities):
- Within 48h: gather artifacts, confirm hardware RMA or replacement status, verify post-repair smoke tests.
- Within 7 days: lead a short RCA (1 page) covering root cause hypothesis, mitigations applied, gaps in monitoring, and long-term next steps.
- Proposed mitigations to consider: better per-GPU isolation in device-plugin, automated per-GPU draining mechanism, and extended preflight GPU diagnostics before scheduling.

Open notes and TODOs (working items):
- TODO: write automated detection play (Linear RED-2309) to mark per-GPU trouble and auto-taint node for new allocs only.
- TODO: coordinate with HW vendor to get more granular NVLink error codes into metrics.
- Question: can we safely use `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` under warm containers? Need test matrix. (Assign: Miguel)

Appendix: quick heuristics for oncall
- If errors spike and recovery rate >1/minute across multiple hosts -> escalate immediately.
- If single GPU shows repeated ECC ULC that persists after reset -> plan for replacement.
- If node exhibits filesystem I/O errors alongside GPU errors -> treat as high risk and drain the node.

End of draft.

Notes: informal style intended; replace with formal runbook after validation and dry-run. Keep this doc as a short, searchable cheat-sheet for oncall while we build the longer field-guide.
